newsitem.title: BRAZIL: MOTOR RACING-EVER-POPULAR STEWART RETURNS TO BRAZIL.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-EVER-POPULAR STEWART RETURNS TO BRAZIL.

text.p: Jackie Stewart returned to Brazil for a motor race for the first time since 1973 on Wednesday and was recognised instantly.
As he queued at Rio de Janeiro airport to pay his airport tax, an official manning the desk looked up and said: "Ah, Mr Jackie! I hope you can help (Rubens) Barrichello in your team now."
Stewart, now a grandfather and owner of a new Grand Prix team, remains one of the world's most recognisable and affable sports personalities.
He is as popular in Brazil as he is in Australia, as he remains in Britain and as he has always been in the United States. And it is easy to see why.
On the long trip from London to Sao Paulo, including a two-hour stop in Rio, the three-times world drivers' champion never complained once.
The journey was hot, the service was hardly first class and there was a lot of queuing.
And on top of that, Stewart, along with an exhausted group of other Grand Prix travellers, had to wait by the Rio carousel to collect his own bags and haul them down to the next check-in counter.

"The last time I came down here was for Ayrton's funeral," he recalled, remembering how in 1994 he acted as pall-bearer at the emotional funeral of Brazil's Ayrton Senna, an event which brought the vast metropolis of Sao Paulo to a halt.
"I also used to come down to Rio in the 1980s to do some television work but I have not been here for a race at Interlagos since I last raced here in 1973."

In that race, Stewart qualified eighth and finished second behind local hero Emerson Fittipaldi, a result he would love to see repeated on Sunday by either of his two drivers -- Brazilian Barrichello or Jan Magnussen of Denmark.
With Barrichello in his team, Stewart is assured of popularity in Latin America.
But he is not about to get carried away, despite his team's encouraging debut in Australia three weeks ago.
Barrichello qualified in 11th place in Melbourne and although he failed to finish the race he drove strongly and competitively for most of it.
"We must be careful not to set our sights too high after Rubens excellent qualifying effort in Melbourne," he warned. "It was unrealistic in my view to have out-qualified both Jordans.
"We've had little testing since then, alas, so we don't come to South America with very high expectations. But the whole team is totally focused on gaining more knowledge.
"And I remember that 1973 race well. Emerson and I had just been on holiday together. It was a good second place for me too, as the car wasn't up to it that day."
